identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Meenakshi Amman Temple is one of the few major South Indian temples where the goddess, not her consort, is the principal deity: Meenakshi's shrine stands at the centre of the innermost courtyard and is worshipped before Sundareswarar's. It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, one of the 276 Shaiva sites hymned in the Tevaram, and its annual Meenakshi Tirukalyanam re-enacts the marriage of the goddess to Shiva as the ritual centre of the city of Madurai.

governance.managingAuthority: Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Nadu

narrative.documentedHistory:
The earliest surviving masonry of the complex is attributed to the Pandya emperor Sadayavarman Kulasekaran I (r. 1190-1216), with later Pandya rulers extending the temple through the thirteenth century. The temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the 276 Shaiva shrines praised in the Tevaram hymns of the Nayanars, which places worship at the site well before the surviving fabric.

After the death of Maravarman Kulasekhara I in 1310, Madurai was raided in 1311 by Malik Kafur of the Delhi Sultanate and the temple was heavily damaged and looted. The Vijayanagara Empire recovered Madurai in 1378; Kumara Kampana is credited with rebuilding parts of the complex and reconsecrating images that had been concealed.

The present layout is largely the work of the Madurai Nayaks. Vishwanatha Nayak (r. 1529-1564) is associated with the gilding of the Meenakshi vimana and with the thousand-pillared hall, and Tirumala Nayaka (r. 1623-1655) added the Vasantha mandapa. Over forty inscriptions in the complex document endowments and building phases.
narrative.architectureStyle: Dravidian, largely of the Madurai Nayak period
narrative.sacredTank: Potramarai Kulam (Golden Lotus tank), approximately 165 ft by 120 ft
narrative.inscriptionsSummary: More than forty inscriptions are recorded in the complex, documenting its construction phases and endowments.

visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Same-day timings, pooja changes and festival closures should be confirmed with the HR&CE temple office on 04522344360 or via maduraimeenakshi.hrce.tn.gov.in, since the department states that pooja timings change during festivals.

openingHours.notes: As published on the HR&CE temple page; the department notes timings may vary during festival periods.
HR&CE publishes the evening session as 4:00 PM to 10:00 PM. The temple is closed between 12:30 PM and 4:00 PM.

poojas.description: The closing pooja of the day, after which the temple shuts.

festivals.significance: The re-enactment of the marriage of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, the principal annual festival of the temple and of the city of Madurai.
festivals.processionOrRituals: Includes the Ther Thiruvizha, in which decorated temple cars are drawn by devotees through the concentric streets surrounding the temple.
festivals.notes: Duration is reported inconsistently: the HR&CE temple page describes an annual 10-day Meenakshi Tirukalyanam festival, while Wikipedia describes a 15-day celebration in the month of Chithirai. Recorded here without a settled duration.

shrines.locationDescription: In the innermost courtyard, set more centrally than the Sundareswarar sanctum, reflecting the goddess's primacy at this temple. Its vimana was gilded under Vishwanatha Nayak.
In the innermost courtyard, parallel to the Meenakshi sanctum.
A colonnaded tank of roughly 165 ft by 120 ft within the complex, with a gilded lotus at its centre.
A sculpted hall of 985 carved pillars, associated with Vishwanatha Nayak's works; it also houses a temple art museum.
The tallest of the temple's 14 gopurams, built in the late 16th century and rising about 170 ft (52 m), carrying over 1,500 sculpted mythological figures.
Hall added to the complex by Tirumala Nayaka (r. 1623-1655).
